PART 1 - Dashboard (dashboard/). A static page, plain HTML, CSS and JS with no framework and no build step, that polls run.json and ledger.json from a configurable location (default: the same directory) every couple of seconds and re-renders. It never writes anything. It is the main thing judges see in the demo video, so it must tell the story on its own:
- A budget bar: spent against remaining, updating live.
- One row per task: title, size, the tier chosen, the one-sentence decision reason in plain words, cost so far against its ceiling, and status (pending, running, passed, failed, skipped). A task that was stopped at its ceiling and escalated must be unmistakable: the stopped attempt and the continued attempt both visible.
- A headline number: cost per merged PR, with the baseline figure beside it when a baseline run is supplied.
- The ledger: one row per attempt with model, tokens, cost, result, and links to the PR, the neatlogs trace and the Entire checkpoint when present.
- A strip showing which integrations are on, off or broken (neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai, GitHub).
- Works from the fixture with no server-side code; include a tiny script that replays the fixture over ~60 seconds as a simulated live run so the page can be seen moving.
Design: use the frontend-design skill. Visual direction is an accountant's ledger, not a SaaS dashboard: warm cream paper, ink black, ruled lines, a serif display face plus a monospace for figures, and ONE accent colour, vermilion red, used only for overspend, stops and the Tally mark. No gradients, glows, cards-on-dark or neon. The mark is a tally: four upright strokes crossed by one red diagonal slash. It must be readable in a 1080p screen recording and usable at laptop width. Verify it in the browser (ao preview / ao browser) and look at the result before reporting.

PART 2 - Demo material (demo/).
- demo/sample-backlog.yaml: a small self-contained sample backlog (6-7 tasks of mixed size, one that looks medium but is hard, one unsolvable) with scripted outcomes, for `tally demo`, which runs simulated workers and needs no accounts or keys. Lane A builds the runner; you provide the data in the schema's format.
- demo/fly-doom-jev-backlog.yaml: a DRAFT backlog of 7 real tasks for the target repo https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/fly-doom-jev (3 small, 3 medium, 1 that looks medium but is hard). Each task needs a title, an issue-style description specific enough for an agent, the expected size, and a concrete pass check (an existing or new pytest that must pass). Use lane A's findings on which tests run in a fresh checkout. Do NOT create issues on, push to, or otherwise change fly-doom-jev on GitHub; this file is a draft for the user to approve.

PUBLISHING IS AUTHORISED for this repo only: push your branch to origin (Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack) and open PRs against main, one per coherent piece, small commits. Never print, log or commit anything from ~/.tally/.env. Do not create plan or analysis documents in the repo. # Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

S1 AO spawn/read/kill: YES, fully scriptable.
- Spawn: `ao spawn --project neatlogs-hack --harness claude-code --model claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 --name tally-spike-s1-haiku --prompt "...Reply PONG..."` -> `spawned session neatlogs-hack-3 "tally-spike-s1-haiku" (idle)`. - Status: `ao session get <id> --json` -> {session:{id,harness,status,activity:{state,lastActivityAt},isTerminated,branch,branchState:{commits,unpushed},prs:[]}}. Observed status "working"/activity "active" then "idle"/"idle" ~13 s after spawn (Haiku) and ~19 s (Codex). `ao session ls --json -p neatlogs-hack --include-terminated` lists them (orchestrators only with -a). - Result: there is NO transcript/output endpoint (GET /api/v1/sessions/<id>/messages|transcript|output|events all 404). "idle" only means the turn ended, not that the task succeeded. Tally must judge by branch/PR + its own test run (as planned). The Haiku reply "PONG" was confirmed only by reading the Claude transcript file under ~/.claude/projects/<worktree-path>/.
- Kill: `ao session kill neatlogs-hack-3` -> "session neatlogs-hack-3 killed", then status "terminated", isTerminated true. Both test sessions are killed.
- Bad model is rejected up front: `--model not-a-real-model` -> "model ... is not in the active provider catalog (UNSUPPORTED_MODEL)".

Which codex id is which tier is my reading of the names, not something AO states.

S2 usage endpoint shape (GET /api/v1/usage/sessions/{id}):
{sessionId, incomplete, totals:{inputTokens, cachedInputTokens, uncachedInputTokens, outputTokens, processedTokens, cacheReadTokens, estimatedCost}, harnesses:[{harness, totals, models:[{modelId, totals}]}]}. estimatedCost = null or {totalNanos, inputNanos, cachedInputNanos, outputNanos, coverage:"complete"|"partial", providerAttribution:"observed"}; unit is nanos of USD (1e9 = $1). List form /api/v1/usage/sessions -> {sessions:[{sessionId, processedTokens, totalTokens, incomplete, estimatedCost}]}.
- inputTokens includes cached; Claude cache-WRITE tokens are folded into uncachedInputTokens (Haiku test: 10 input + 16,874 cache-creation in the transcript = 16,884 uncached in AO). AO does not expose cache writes separately.
- Codex: estimatedCost populated within ~10 s (gpt-5.6-luna test: 21,606 tokens -> totalNanos 2,345,760 = $0.0023; implies $0.20/M input, $0.02/M cached, $1.20/M output).
- Claude Code: NOT reliable. Haiku session: estimatedCost null (tokens present). Across all sessions on this daemon: claude-opus-5-5 has cost on 17 sessions and null on 1 (this live session, still null at 660k tokens); claude-haiku-4-5 null on its only session. Also all totals were null for the first ~30-40 s of the Haiku session.
- Consequence: the watcher can poll tokens, but Tally must compute cost itself as tokens x list price from tally.yaml and treat AO's estimatedCost as optional. Ceilings cannot fire in the first ~30 s of a worker.

S3 neatlogs:
- Read API exists: https://app.neatlogs.com/api/v1/public/... # ao report

Persist a meaningful worker report for durable delivery to the active project
orchestrator.

## Syntax

```text
ao report <free-form-text>
ao report --checkpoint --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --needs-input --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --stuck --note <text> [output flags]
ao report --done --note <text> [output flags]
```

Output flags are repeatable:

```text
--artifact <opaque-reference>
--pr-created <pr-or-mr-url>
--pr-reviewed <pr-or-mr-url>
```

Use reports for meaningful transitions, decisions, blockers, required input,
outputs, and terminal judgment. Do not narrate routine commands. Outputs do not
imply completion, and `--done` does not terminate the session.

Attach a reviewable deliverable as soon as it is ready, not only at `--done`:
use `--artifact <reference>` on the report for the milestone that produced it.
Examples include a requested document, a rendered dashboard, or another output
the orchestrator or human needs to open directly. `--artifact` takes any opaque
reference string; it is not validated as a URL.
In a chat session, an HTML file from the artifact directory that you attach
with `--artifact` also shows in the thread.

Routine test logs, command output, scratch notes, and intermediate diagnostics
are working material, not deliverables. Do not attach them unless requested or
needed to explain an actionable failure. Summarize validation in the report note;
when a separate deliverable is useful, prefer one consolidated report over
individual logs. Ordinary progress updates and concise final answers do not
need separate artifact files.

Saving a local artifact or attaching its reference to an AO report is not
external publishing authorization. Publish externally only within the
user-authorized scope.

`--pr-created` and `--pr-reviewed` accept complete GitHub PR or GitLab MR URLs.

`--needs-input` requests immediate non-interrupting delivery. `--stuck`
requests immediate delivery plus a rate-limited interrupt. Informational work
batches for up to one hour, while the first done report opens a fixed five
minute settlement window.

**Examples:**

```bash
ao report "The focused tests pass; I am checking the generated diff."
ao report --done --note "Ready for review." \
  --pr-created https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/88
```

     248 README.md
# Tally

A CFO for a fleet of coding agents. Give it a backlog and a budget. It sizes
each task, sends it to the cheapest model likely to finish it, stops any task
that overruns its spend ceiling, hands failed work to a stronger model, and
ends with a ledger tying spend to each attempt, its test result and any opened PR.

Status: early build, available from GitHub. The npm package `tally-agents`
has not been released yet. The seven-task demo uses simulated workers; real
runs use Agent Orchestrator and record their attempts and evidence separately.

## Install

Prerequisites before you install:

- Node 20 or later and npm.
- Git for installation from GitHub or a source checkout.
- For real runs: Agent Orchestrator installed and running, with at least one
  signed-in coding agent it can start.
- For real runs: GitHub CLI installed and signed in with `gh auth login`.

The simulated demo and dashboard need only Node and npm. They do not need an
AO account, coding-agent login or GitHub credentials.

Three ways in:

1. **GitHub (available now):** `npm install -g github:Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack#release`.
   The `release` branch includes the compiled CLI and records its source commit
   in `release-source.json`; no TypeScript or manual build is needed. The main
   branch is source-only and is not the global-install target.
2. **npm (not released yet):** after release, `npm install -g tally-agents`.
3. **Source checkout:** `git clone https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack`,
   enter `neatlogs-hack`, and run `npm install` followed by `npm run build`.
   Then use `node bin/tally.js` in place of `tally` in the commands below.
   After editing TypeScript sources, run `npm run build` again. Generated
   `dist/` files are not committed to main.

The npm package is named `tally-agents`; the installed command is still
`tally`.

Maintainers can build a release tree with
`npm run release:branch -- --source origin/main --out /tmp/tally-release`.
Add `--push` to update the dedicated `release` branch (never publishes to npm).
The main-push workflow builds and smoke-checks that tree before updating it.
`npm run test:git-install` checks the GitHub `#release` URL with an empty cache
and temporary global prefix, then checks version, help, demo and dashboard
outside the checkout. Pass another Git URL after `--` to check a candidate.

## Quickstart

After either global installation, start in an empty directory:

```bash
tally demo
tally dashboard
```

The demo writes `.tally/runs/` in that directory. Open the URL printed by
`tally dashboard`; it reads the latest run and lists recorded runs. Keep it
running while viewing the page, and press Ctrl-C to stop it. If its default
port is occupied, use `tally dashboard --port 0` for a free port.

`tally demo --live` keeps workers simulated while checking the configured
read-only integrations. Bundled cfo.ai workspace/table values are placeholders;
missing credentials are reported, and no real worker is launched.

### A Provided Tarball

With only a packed `tally-agents-0.1.0.tgz` in your current directory, these
commands install into a temporary prefix without changing your normal global
installation, then follow the same quickstart:

```bash
npm install -g --prefix "$PWD/tally-install" ./tally-agents-0.1.0.tgz
export PATH="$PWD/tally-install/bin:$PATH"
tally demo
tally dashboard --port 0
```

No checkout, manual build or `tally init` is needed for the demo.

### Your Repository

Run `tally init` from the repository you want Tally to work on. It asks for
budget and issue label; neatlogs, Entire and cfo.ai are separate opt-in prompts,
defaulting to No. It displays the proposed `tally.yaml`, install record in
`.tally/`, AO project registration/configuration and setup hook, then asks for
final confirmation (default No) before applying changes. Use `tally init
--dry-run` to preview without applying, or `--yes` only when you consent to
applying detected defaults without prompts. Review model tiers, prices, tests
and ceilings before starting workers. Scoped worker allow-list enforcement is
not yet installed; init does not change global coding-agent settings.

Init detects test/setup commands from repository evidence and proposes tiers
only for installed Codex or Claude Code agents. When no test command is found,
it asks for a shell command: Tally cannot verify work without one. Blank input
or `--yes` with no detected test command fails without writing configuration
or changing AO settings. An undetected setup command is optional and never
guessed.

Use `tally doctor`, then `tally run --plan` to inspect routing without spawning
workers. A real `tally run` starts workers and can publish verified branches
and pull requests. `tally run --dry-run` uses simulated workers instead.

`tally uninstall` lists the files and AO settings it owns and asks for
confirmation before removing them. It refuses to overwrite edits made since
init. It leaves run history, credentials and the globally installed CLI in
place; remove that CLI separately with `npm uninstall -g tally-agents`.

### Static Snapshot

`tally publish --out site` writes a self-contained static dashboard,
defaulting to real recorded runs. Select folders explicitly with
`tally publish --out site --runs run-id-1,run-id-2`; use this for simulated demo
data. It scans exported files for sensitive content and prints file sizes and
the total. Serve the directory on a static HTTP host, including under a
sub-path. This creates local files and does not deploy them.

During development, `npm run tally -- <command>` runs the CLI from source.

For routine validation, run:

```bash
npm test
```

## Commands

| Command | What it will do |
|---|---|
| `tally run` | Run the backlog against the budget in `tally.yaml`. Flags: `--dry-run`, `--budget <usd>`, `--only <task>`, `--baseline`, `--config <path>`, `--plan`, `--dashboard`/`--open`. |
| `tally experiment` | Run simulated baseline and Tally modes with `--dry-run --repeats N` (default 2). Real experiment execution is currently gated. `--budget <usd>` is the aggregate safety cap. Baseline keeps no per-task ceiling; real worker base validation and safety monitoring are implemented but have not been exercised live. |
| `tally demo` | Run the full loop with simulated workers on `demo/tally.yaml` and `demo/sample-backlog.yaml`. No accounts or keys. Writes `.tally/runs/<run-id>/run.json` and `ledger.json`; add `--dashboard` for the one-command demo, or `--live` to light up read-only integrations while workers stay fake. |
| `tally dashboard` | Serve `dashboard/` and `.tally/runs/` read-only on `127.0.0.1`. The printed URL passes `?data=/runs/latest/` so the page reads the stable latest-run mirror. |
| `tally init` | Preview files and AO changes, then ask final default-No consent. `--dry-run` previews; `--yes` applies defaults without prompts. Scoped worker allow-list enforcement is not yet installed. |
| `tally uninstall` | Confirm removal of init-owned configuration and AO settings; preserve history and credentials. |
| `tally doctor` | One line per integration: connected, missing or broken, with the fix. |
| `tally login cfoai` | Sign in to cfo.ai; tokens are cached outside the repository. |
| `tally traces drain --run <id>` | Recover only that finished run's worker traces, verify readable spans, then update saved status and worker trace ids. Use `--output <run-dir>` for a run stored elsewhere. |
| `tally market --limit 5` | Search CrustData for companies adopting coding agents; requires its credentials. |
| `tally publish --out site` | Static dashboard export with a sensitive-content scan. No deployment. |

## Layout

Experiment summaries are atomically updated after each completed run at
`.tally/runs/experiments/<experimentId>/summary.json`. The dashboard server lists
them in `/runs/index.json` under `experiments`. Each underlying run retains its
own folder, `mode`, and `repeat`. Simulated cost remains labeled as simulated.
The aggregate watcher polls once a second; reported final cost can exceed the
stop threshold due to polling or metering lag and is never clipped to the cap.

| Folder | Holds |
|---|---|
| `schema/` | The contract every part reads: TypeScript types, JSON Schema, validators, and a sample finished run in `schema/fixtures/finished-run/`. |
| `engine/` | The run loop, run state and ledger. |
| `adapters/` | One thin module per outside tool (Agent Orchestrator, Entire, neatlogs, cfo.ai, GitHub). |
| `agent/` | The CFO agent: sizing, routing, ceilings, escalation. |
| `cli/` | The `tally` command. |
| `dashboard/` | Static page that reads the ledger and run state. |
| `demo/` | Sample backlog and scripted outcomes for `tally demo`. |

## Configuration

With neatlogs on, Tally drains the completed Codex worker's hook spool from
its own process, outside the worker sandbox. It uses the official package's
spool API (there is no flush CLI), matching native session IDs or the worktree
path. Only successfully delivered batches are acknowledged; failed,
unrelated and malformed batches remain queued. A locked or incomplete drain
is reported as missing worker trace delivery. Dry runs do not drain workers.

With `integrations.entire: true`, enable Entire in the target repository and
trust its Codex hooks through `/hooks` before starting workers. Tally records
the task commit's `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer and its native `entireSessionId`
separately from the AO `sessionId`. Logs-only checkpoints retain conversation
context; escalation defaults to a metadata-only handoff containing the
checkpoint/session IDs, branch, recorded and changed files, attempt verdict,
and task text. It does not generate a summary or export a transcript.
`entire.generatedSummaries: true` explicitly opts into Entire's summary
provider (`checkpoint explain --generate`), which may export session content;
this setting is off by default and requires the user's approval.
When Tally publishes a verified branch, it also pushes the checkpoint refs
named by its new commits to `origin` and to an `entire` remote when configured.
Checkpoint upload failures are reported as publishing failures. Dry runs do
not publish branches or checkpoints.

Entire documents commit links as
`https://entire.io/gh/<org>/<repo>/commit/<commit-sha>`. Tally keeps
`checkpointUrl` null unless the CLI returns a URL; a local checkpoint does not
by itself establish that a hosted link works.

Tally assumes nothing about the repository it works on. The repository, test
command, model tiers, list prices, ceilings and budget all come from
`tally.yaml` (a tier is a name, harness, model id, provider, list price and ceiling share); see `schema/fixtures/finished-run/tally.yaml` for a complete
example and `schema/tally-config.schema.json` for the rules.

Money in the ledger and run state is stored as integer nanos of USD
(1 USD = 1,000,000,000). List-price estimates multiply aggregate tokens by the
configured rates in `tally.yaml`; they are normalized estimates, not invoices.
New ledger rows snapshot those rates in `price` and record their source and
verification status in `priceNote`. Unknown models/providers or rates that
disagree with the verified snapshot are labelled unverified. Operator-supplied
`tiers[].priceNote` is retained as a config note, not independently verified.

### Codex Tier Prices

Official base text rates checked 2026-10-11, USD per million tokens:

| Model | Input | Cached Input | Output | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| gpt-5.6-luna | 0.20 | 0.02 | 1.20 | [OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.6-luna) |
| gpt-5.6-terra | 2.00 | 0.20 | 12.00 | [OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.6-terra) |
| gpt-5.6-sol | 4.00 | 0.40 | 20.00 | [OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.6-sol) |

```yaml
tiers:
  - { name: cheap, harness: codex, sessionMode: tui, provider: openai, model: gpt-5.6-luna, price: { inputUsdPerMTok: 0.2, cachedInputUsdPerMTok: 0.02, outputUsdPerMTok: 1.2 }, ceilingFraction: 0.2 }
  - { name: middle, harness: codex, sessionMode: tui, provider: openai, model: gpt-5.6-terra, price: { inputUsdPerMTok: 2, cachedInputUsdPerMTok: 0.2, outputUsdPerMTok: 12 }, ceilingFraction: 0.5 }
  - { name: top, harness: codex, sessionMode: tui, provider: openai, model: gpt-5.6-sol, price: { inputUsdPerMTok: 4, cachedInputUsdPerMTok: 0.4, outputUsdPerMTok: 20 }, ceilingFraction: 1 }
```

Per-request prompts above 272K input tokens have input/output uplifts;
cache writes also have an uplift. AO's aggregate token buckets cannot resolve
these adjustments. Sol's published promotional rates last at least through
2026-11-21; recheck before subsequent runs. Historical costs are not repriced.

For dry runs, set `backlog.source: file` and point `backlog.file` at YAML like:

```yaml
tasks:
  - id: T1
    title: Add validation for empty player name
    size: small
    outcomes: [passed]
  - id: T2
    title: Persist settings after restart
    size: medium
    outcomes: [stopped, passed]
```

`outcomes` is optional and defaults to one passed simulated attempt.

The latest run is also mirrored to `.tally/runs/latest/run.json` and
`.tally/runs/latest/ledger.json` so the dashboard has one stable path to poll.

## Secrets

Keys live in `~/.tally/.env`, outside every repository, and are loaded from
there. Never put them in this repo; `.env` files are git-ignored.

+or file operation fails, it lists confirmed changes and unwritten files and
+prints the exact init command to resume. Re-running resumes only its owned,
+unchanged files; edited configs or changed AO settings are never overwritten.
+The recovery record is removed after init and doctor complete. This is a
+recoverable transaction, not an atomic transaction spanning the AO daemon and
+the filesystem: an interrupted call may require checking its outcome.

- `t1.png` to `t4.png`: the aesthetic he chose. 1980s airbrush advertising: a hyper-real product as hero on a deep gradient backdrop (black, indigo, violet), glossy highlights, water droplets and star glints, surreal scale (giant cups as desert monuments under a crimson-pink sky), a mascot with attitude in a white suit, print grain.
- `tally-logo-reference.png`: the Tally mark and wordmark. Four black hand-drawn strokes, two eye dots, one orange-red slash, "Meet Tally / the CFO for your agent fleet" in a high-contrast serif on lined cream paper.
- `ao-mascot.png`, `ao-logo.svg`: Agent Orchestrator's mascot (glossy blue blocky creature holding a conductor's baton) and logo, from `Untrivial-ai/agent-orchestrator` (Apache-2.0). Use it as supplied; do not redraw or restyle another project's character beyond placement, scale and simple motion.

## What it is

A static site in a new `site/` folder at the repo root. No heavy framework: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript like the dashboard, or a tiny build step only if it clearly pays for itself. It must deploy to Vercel as a static folder with no server. Nothing in `site/` may be added to the npm package (`package.json` `files` already excludes it; keep it that way and check with `npm pack --dry-run`).

## Sections, top to bottom

1. **Hero.** The Tally mark draws itself the way the CLI animation does: four strokes top to bottom, eyes appear and blink, the orange slash strikes across, then "Meet Tally, the CFO for your agent fleet." The mark should feel like the airbrushed product in the reference tiles (chrome/enamel sheen, glint), on a black-to-indigo backdrop. Build it as SVG so it animates crisply; an airbrushed hero image will be supplied later as an optional layer (see Artwork).
2. **Install, the centrepiece.** A large `npm install -g tally-agents` with a working copy button. Beside it a terminal window replaying the real CLI: reuse the actual frames from `cli/logo.ts` (do not fake a different animation), followed by a short, truthful `tally init` / `tally run` excerpt. Links: https://www.npmjs.com/package/tally-agents and the GitHub repo.
3. **What Tally does.** One animated flow of five steps, in these words or close to them: routes GitHub issues to a cost-effective model, caps spend per task, escalates if needed, verifies the change, opens a pull request. Tally never merges.
4. **Three toggles.** Entire, neatlogs and cfo.ai, each an on/off switch. One sample run (a ledger row plus a small dashboard card) re-draws as each is flipped. Use only true behaviour:
   - Entire off: task sized by a search of the repository. On: sized from the code graph; a checkpoint is attached to each commit.
   - neatlogs off: no trace. On: a decision trace and a worker trace id on every ledger row.
   - cfo.ai off: budget typed into `tally.yaml`. On: live monthly budget read from cfo.ai, spend written back and reconciled to the ledger.
   Take the sample values from a real run, e.g. `schema/fixtures/finished-run/` or the proof numbers below. Do not invent savings percentages.
5. **Agent Orchestrator.** The AO mascot and the Tally mark working together (for example AO conducting with its baton while tally strokes line up and get struck through). Message: with Agent Orchestrator, Tally runs agents in parallel; without it, Tally runs Claude Code or Codex directly, one task at a time. Tally detects AO at `tally init`.
6. **Onboarding video.** A styled placeholder frame (80s TV or ad-frame treatment) with a clear "video coming" state, built so one file path or embed URL switches it to the real video.
7. **Proof.** Real numbers only, each linked: four runner paths each proven by a real run on `Vaibhaav-Tiwari/chip-design-groundup`: Codex via AO (PR #10, $0.012), Claude Code via AO (PR #13, $0.087), Claude Code direct (PR #14, $0.077), Codex direct (PR #18, $0.011). Stop-at-ceiling and escalation proven once (fly-doom-jev PR #14). 662 tests. State nothing that is not in the README.
8. **Contact card.** "Contact us": email vaibhaavtiwari@gmail.com, X https://x.com/battarchicken (@battarchicken), plus npm and GitHub links. Styled like the white-suit mascot tile if artwork allows.

## Animation

Wanted and substantial: the hero draw-in and blink; the replayed terminal; scroll-triggered section reveals; toggles re-drawing the sample run; star glints and droplets catching light; parallax in the desert scene; mascots moving in a loop. Use CSS, SVG and the Web Animations API or one small library from a CDN. Everything must stop under `prefers-reduced-motion`, and the page must be fully readable with JavaScript off.

## Artwork

Code cannot paint airbrush illustration. The orchestrator is generating the painted images (hero object, crimson-sky desert scene, mascots together, contact-card figure) and will drop them into the reference folder as they are approved. Build every section so it looks finished with CSS/SVG alone (gradients, glints, grain, type), with a clearly named image slot per section that upgrades it when the file exists. Do not block on artwork and do not generate images yourself.

## Quality bar

- Responsive from 360 px wide; no horizontal scroll; fast (no multi-megabyte scripts; compress images, lazy-load below the fold).
- Real type: a heavy 80s display face for headlines and the high-contrast serif for "Meet Tally" (Google Fonts are fine). Open Graph and Twitter card tags, favicon from the Tally mark.
- Accessible: contrast, focus states, alt text, keyboard-operable toggles.
- Look at it yourself in the AO browser panel (`ao preview`, `ao browser`; read the using-ao preview and browser guides) at desktop and phone widths before reporting. Say plainly what you could not check.

## How to deliver

- Milestone 1 (report to the orchestrator and stop for review): hero and install sections complete and animated, the rest stubbed in the right order. Open a PR, give the preview path.
- Milestone 2: remaining sections.
- Small PRs; the orchestrator gates and merges. Do not deploy; deployment to Vercel is done by Vaibhaav from his account after review.

InstallWhat it doesTogglesProofContact

Meet Tally

the CFO for your agent fleet

Hand it your GitHub issues and a budget. It picks a cost-effective model for each one, stops any task at its spend ceiling, and opens a pull request only when your tests pass.

Install Tally

One line and it is on your machine.

$ npm install -g tally-agents

Needs Node 20 or later. The package is tally-agents; the command it installs is tally. Then, in an empty folder:

tally demo        # seven simulated tasks, no accounts or keys
tally dashboard   # watch the ledger fill in

tally-agents on npmSource on GitHub

What Tally does

  1. Routes each GitHub issue to a cost-effective model.
  2. Caps spend per task.
  3. Escalates to a stronger model if needed.
  4. Verifies the change with your tests.
  5. Opens a pull request. Tally never merges.

The animated flow for this section is being built.

Three switches

  • Entire. Off: a task is sized by a search of the repository. On: sized from the code graph, with a checkpoint attached to each commit.
  • neatlogs. Off: no trace. On: a decision trace and a worker trace id on every ledger row.
  • cfo.ai. Off: the budget is typed into tally.yaml. On: the live monthly budget is read from cfo.ai, and spend is written back and reconciled to the ledger.

The working switches and the sample run they redraw are being built.

With Agent Orchestrator, or without

With Agent Orchestrator, Tally runs agents in parallel. Without it, Tally runs Claude Code or Codex directly, one task at a time. tally init detects which you have.

The scene with the Agent Orchestrator mascot is being built.

See a first run

The onboarding video is not recorded yet. Its frame is being built.

Proof, with receipts

Each of the four ways Tally can run an agent has completed a real run on Vaibhaav-Tiwari/chip-design-groundup:

  • Codex through Agent Orchestrator: pull request #10, $0.012.
  • Claude Code through Agent Orchestrator: pull request #13, $0.087.
  • Claude Code direct: pull request #14, $0.077.
  • Codex direct: pull request #18, $0.011.

The full proof section is being built.

Contact us

  • X @battarchicken
  • tally-agents on npm
  • Source on GitHub

11 Oct 2026, 23:10 IST. Vaibhaav rejected version 1 completely: the 80s airbrush direction, the painted images, the heavy display fonts, the chrome logo and both mascot treatments. ## The Tally mark

Use the mark he approved: `site-reference-v2/tally-mark-approved.png`. It is the terminal rendering from `cli/logo.ts`: four white block strokes of uneven height, two small square eyes, one orange stepped slash, "Meet" in italic mono, "Tally" in block letters, "the CFO for your agent fleet", on dark slate. That pixel/terminal mark **is** the logo and the mascot. Render it crisply (SVG rects or a canvas from the real frames), animate it with the same draw-in the CLI uses, and use it at small size for the nav and favicon. No chrome, no gradients on the mark, no hand-drawn variant, no painted version.

The repo is now `OrchestratorInc/agent-orchestrator`.

- One calm base. Dark slate close to the mark's own background works with the mark and with orchestrator.inc; a light or cream section for the judges block is fine if it reads better. One accent only: the mark's orange.
- Type: one refined serif for display with italic for emphasis (in the manner of wisprflow), one clean sans for body and UI (Inter, Geist or similar), one mono for code and eyebrow labels. No novelty or heavy rounded faces. A clear scale and generous line height.
- Show the real product: the dashboard (from `tally demo` and `tally dashboard`), the terminal, a ledger row, the code graph view. Capture real screenshots and frame them like orchestrator.inc does. No stock art, no generated illustration, no ray bursts, glints or grain.

1. **Hero**: the mark animating, one line of what Tally is, the install command with copy button, "Read the getting-started guide" (https://github.com/Vaibhaav-Tiwari/neatlogs-hack/blob/main/docs/GETTING_STARTED.md) and npm/GitHub links.

content.text:
The parallel-run edit is made and committed locally, but nothing is pushed: my last command to push, open a PR and report was declined by the human, so I'm holding all outward actions until told to go.

**Already live**
- **Production URL:** https://tally-agents-pi.vercel.app/ — project `tally-agents` in his personal scope, a CLI deploy of main at `2015d09`, static with no build step.
- **Do not share `tally-agents.vercel.app`** (without `-pi`): that address is someone else's unrelated site.
- **GitHub connection:** `vercel link --yes` connected the GitHub repository on its own, against the instruction. I ran `vercel git disconnect` immediately, before any deploy, and it confirmed the disconnect. Please check that the project's Git settings show no repository.
- **Local env file:** the same command wrote `site/.env.local`; I deleted it without opening it.
- **Nothing extra:** no domain, analytics or add-on was attached, and nothing asked for payment.
- **Verified from outside in headless Chrome:**
  - HTTP 200 over HTTPS, all assets and the three font families load.
  - No console errors and no `http://` references at 1440 and 390 px.
  - The copy button works, the terminal replays, and the phone menu opens.
  - The page loads with scripts off.
  - The getting-started, GitHub and X links return 200. The npm web page answers 403 to curl (its bot block); the registry confirms `tally-agents` exists.

**Committed locally on `ao/neatlogs-hack-6/site-deploy`, not pushed**
- **Share image:** a 1200×630 image made from the pixel mark, with Open Graph tags pointing at the production address.
- **Ignore rules:** `.vercel/` is git-ignored, and `site/tools/` is kept out of deploys.
- **Agent Orchestrator card and headline:** now say Tally can run agents in parallel through AO, opt-in with `tally run --parallel 3`, each in its own session and worktree, with each task's ceiling reserved before it starts. The "without it" card says parallel needs AO.
- **Judges 30% block:** a new card for `run-20261011-190131Z` with the three issues, PRs #24, #23 and #22 with their costs, the $0.0411 total against a $2.00 cap, the 70-second overlap, and "cfo.ai spend rose by exactly the ledger total". Parallel is removed from the "not proven" list. It makes no claim about overshoot or the direct runner, and says nothing about traces for this run.

I have not rendered the new card in a browser yet. Production still serves the old wording and has no share image.

To proceed I need a go-ahead for three things: push this branch, open one PR for both changes, and redeploy with `vercel deploy --prod` once it is merged. If the earlier command was declined for a specific reason (the push, the PR, or the report text), tell me which and I'll adjust.
